The gaming console is notoriously CPU intensive, because your computer has to jump through a lot of hoops to figure out what all the dozens or hundreds of players close enough to affect you are doing. You're getting a 300m radius of data from infantry, and up to 900m depending on vehicles (larger vehicles render furthest, because of their size).

The gaming system has its own unique flight model to compensate for the low flight ceiling but comparatively large map. Because literally every aircraft is capable of vertical takeoff and landing, a specialized combat maneuver called the reverse maneuver has been developed. I can't give exact instructions because I'm a player on a different platform, but the general idea is to slow down, perform a 180-degree roll until your underside faces up, pitch down, then, once level, activate the boost. If you've slowed down sufficiently, the boosters will switch to hover mode, which provides a significant increase in upward thrust.

The maneuver is useful for two reasons: it allows you to face your opponent without engaging in a tedious turning fight, and your speed during the boost phase is high enough, in a peculiar direction, that your opponent will miss many of their shots trying to hit you.

Dogfighting, in general, tends to occur after both pilots have switched to hover mode, enabling them to aim at their opponents while also tumbling in midair with afterburners to make themselves more difficult to target.

If you know the reverse maneuver and your opponent doesn't, you can make them overshoot you and get behind them.

Do note that the reverse maneuver is best executed behind cover, as slowing down and flipping over makes you an easy target.

To maintain hover mode, only pitch down. It's much faster than pitching up anyway.

At more advanced levels, you can use the reverse maneuver sideways or while navigating around an obstacle.

K selection versus r selection. It would be a heavily male-dominated environment even if there were an equal number of males and females.

Males tend to seek out multiple partners from a genetic perspective to maximize the number of offspring, hoping that some will survive to adulthood (r selection), while females, due to the high energy investment required for child-rearing, often prefer fewer, higher-quality partners to increase the chances of their children reaching adulthood (K-selection).

This is, of course, a significant oversimplification that does not accurately represent any individual and overlooks much of our evolutionary history (mammals generally lean towards k-selection, while other species, like reptiles, tend to favor r-selection). However, it provides a reasonable explanation for many general trends. Specifically, our views on sexual relationships are likely influenced more by our particular cultures, which have evolved due to both genetic and environmental factors.

I am not against funding nuclear, solar, wind, or geothermal. I am a free market capitalist. My problem is the government attacking fossil fuels like they are evil. When a certain political figure says "the greatest threat to national security is global warming," that upsets me. We need to let the market work the way it's supposed to, to develop new technologies that remove pollutants and prevent more from entering the atmosphere.

Have you ever heard of the tragedy of the commons? Or failing that, the prisoner's dilemma? When given a public resource that everyone can exploit equally, while the best overall option would be for everyone to meter their use out, the actual end result is that everyone overexploits that resource, because anyone not doing so gets kicked out of the market. That's an example of market failure. The free market isn't perfect. It's certainly good, in the sense that any human actor trying to do the same thing would fall short, but there are certain places where the government needs to step in. For example, just because there's a market for assassination doesn't mean people should be allowed to buy assassins.

Companies that pollute the environment, whether by dumping chemicals into water sources, harmful gases into the atmosphere, or generating excessive amounts of CO2 cause damage to other people. That's a negative externality. The actual costs of their actions are larger than the costs paid by them for their actions, which prevents the market from reaching a true equilibrium. Letting them do as they please is effectively equal to the government giving them a subsidy for no reason.

If nothing else, for the market to work as it needs to, CO2 absolutely needs to be taxed. The market isn't free without that.

And on the flipside, stuff like research into wind, nuclear, and solar are positive externalities—the benefits they have outweigh the price they fetch. Not subsidizing them is equivalent to the government unfairly taxing them.

Not to mention, due to the fact that energy companies are natural monopolies, the free market can't really be allowed to act on them, or the outcome for customers will be sub-par.
